fields.definition: A control input, wired as a 1/4-inch TRS (tip-ring-sleeve) jack, that reads the position of a passive expression pedal by treating the pedal's internal potentiometer as a variable voltage divider; the host device supplies a reference voltage on one conductor and measures the wiper voltage returned on another to derive a continuous control value.
fields.plain_english: A socket on a pedal, amp, or keyboard that lets you plug in a rocking foot pedal so you can sweep an effect such as volume or wah hands-free, the way a dimmer changes a light.
fields.purpose_function: It gives a musician continuous, real-time foot control over a parameter (volume, wah, filter, delay mix) so both hands stay on the instrument; it exists because performers need to shape effects live while playing.
fields.practical_application: A technician patches an expression pedal to this jack with a TRS cable (a mono TS cable will not work) and confirms the pedal's polarity, resistance, and minimum setting match the host so the full sweep is usable.
common_mistakes: Using a mono TS instrument cable instead of a TRS cable, so the pedal reads no sweep or sticks at one value
Assuming any expression pedal fits any device when pedal resistance/taper and polarity must match the host
Confusing an expression-pedal input with a latching or momentary footswitch input
Leaving the pedal's MIN/heel setting wrong so part of the sweep does nothing
scenario_contexts: Assigning a floor multi-effects unit's expression pedal to sweep delay feedback during a solo
Wiring a keyboard's EXP jack to control filter cutoff live
Troubleshooting a dead expression pedal that turns out to be connected with a TS cable

sources: Roland technical support documentation (DD-200 and RE-2 expression pedal setup, EV-5/BOSS FV-500)
Mission Engineering technical article, Understanding Expression Pedals

fields.definition: The sound radiated outward through the f-shaped openings in the top plate of violin-family instruments and archtop guitars; near the instrument's main air (Helmholtz-type) resonance the enclosed air pumps in and out through these holes, so the f-holes act as the acoustic ports that couple the body cavity's low-frequency output to the surrounding air.
fields.plain_english: The f-shaped slots on a violin or archtop are not just decoration; they are where much of the low end escapes, like the port hole on a bass-reflex speaker cabinet.
fields.purpose_function: The f-holes let the body's internal air resonance radiate efficiently, reinforcing the instrument's lower register; their elongated shape concentrates air motion along the long edges, which radiates that resonance more effectively than a round hole of equal area.
fields.practical_application: When close-miking a violin, cello, or archtop, an engineer accounts for the strong low-frequency energy emerging from the f-holes and avoids aiming a mic straight into one, which over-emphasizes boxy low-mids and captures airflow noise.
common_mistakes: Placing the microphone directly over an f-hole, capturing a boomy, unrepresentative low-mid buildup
Believing the f-holes mainly radiate high frequencies when they dominate the low-frequency air resonance
Assuming the f-holes and the vibrating top plate radiate the same spectrum
scenario_contexts: Choosing mic distance and angle for a cello where f-hole output boosts the low register
Recording an archtop jazz guitar acoustically and balancing f-hole versus top-plate radiation
Explaining why a violin sounds boxy when a clip-on mic sits too close to an f-hole

sources: Acoustics Today (Acoustical Society of America), Gough, Violin Acoustics
Proceedings of the Royal Society A, Nia et al., air-resonance power efficiency in the violin and its ancestors
Fletcher & Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments

fields.definition: The onset transient of a note plucked with the fingertip, flesh, or fingernail rather than a pick; because the finger is a wider, softer, more compliant exciter, it releases the string more gradually and excites fewer strong high harmonics, giving a rounder, less percussive attack than a hard, narrow plectrum.
fields.plain_english: How the very start of a note sounds when you pluck a string with your finger instead of a pick, usually softer and warmer with less of the sharp click a pick gives.
fields.purpose_function: It describes a core tonal and dynamic characteristic the player controls with the picking hand; understanding it lets engineers and players predict a note's transient content and dynamic range.
fields.practical_application: When tracking fingerstyle guitar or bass, an engineer chooses gentler compression settings and mic placement to preserve the softer transient and expects more level variation between fingers than with a pick.
common_mistakes: Over-compressing fingerstyle takes with a very fast attack, flattening the natural dynamic swells that define the style
Assuming fingerstyle always means quieter or duller when nail attack can be very bright and percussive
Confusing the attack (onset transient) with the sustain when describing tone
scenario_contexts: Recording a fingerpicked acoustic ballad where soft attacks must stay intact
Comparing DI tones for pick versus fingerstyle bass in a mix
Coaching a player to use nails versus flesh to change the brightness of the attack

sources: Fletcher & Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments (plucked-string excitation, plectrum versus finger)

fields.definition: An organ pipe that produces sound by aerodynamic (air-jet) excitation rather than a vibrating reed: pressurized wind is forced through a narrow slit called the flue or windway to form a thin air sheet that strikes the sharp upper lip of the pipe's mouth, and the resulting oscillating jet drives the standing wave in the pipe's air column, the same mechanism as a recorder or whistle.
fields.plain_english: The most common kind of organ pipe, which makes sound like a whistle or recorder as air is blown across a sharp edge and the pipe's air column sings, unlike reed pipes that buzz a metal tongue.
fields.purpose_function: Flue pipes generate the organ's principal, flute, and string tone colors; the pipe length sets the pitch while the mouth and jet geometry and the pipe scaling set the timbre and harmonic content.
fields.practical_application: When recording a pipe organ, an engineer positions mics to capture the blend of flue pipes across a division and manages the initial chiff transient and the strong low-frequency fundamentals of large flue ranks.
common_mistakes: Thinking all organ pipes contain a vibrating reed when flue pipes have no reed at all
Assuming a flue pipe's pitch comes from the jet speed rather than the resonant length of the air column
Confusing the chiff (attack transient) with a fault
scenario_contexts: Miking a church pipe organ and balancing flue versus reed stops
Explaining why a Principal or Flute stop speaks like a whistle
Managing the initial chiff transient when recording flue ranks

sources: Fletcher & Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments

fields.definition: The set of coupled mechanical and air resonances of an acoustic guitar's body that amplify and color the strings' vibration; the lowest is the main air (Helmholtz-type) resonance formed by the air mass in the soundhole coupling to the cavity's compliance (commonly near 90 to 110 Hz), followed by the main top-plate (soundboard) resonance and higher body modes.
fields.plain_english: The natural boom notes of a guitar's hollow body, the frequencies where the box and the air inside it ring most easily, which give an acoustic guitar its warmth and low end.
fields.purpose_function: These resonances turn the strings' tiny motion into radiated sound and shape the instrument's low-end response and projection; they exist because the body and enclosed air act as coupled resonators driven through the bridge.
fields.practical_application: Engineers use body resonance to guide mic placement, aiming near the 12th fret rather than straight at the soundhole to avoid the boomy main-air peak, and may notch it with EQ when it dominates the low-mids.
common_mistakes: Miking straight into the soundhole and capturing an unbalanced, boomy main-air resonance
Assuming the body resonance is a single frequency rather than several coupled modes
Cutting the low end broadly with EQ instead of notching the specific resonant peak
scenario_contexts: Positioning a small-diaphragm condenser off the 12th fret to tame the body resonance
Diagnosing a boomy note on a dreadnought during tracking
Explaining why a guitar sounds boxy in a small room near its air-resonance frequency

sources: Fletcher & Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments

fields.definition: A passive treble-cut control on an electric or electro-acoustic guitar consisting of a potentiometer in series with a fixed capacitor, wired to shunt the high-frequency portion of the pickup signal to ground; rolling the control down lets more treble bleed away, forming a variable low-pass filter that darkens the tone.
fields.plain_english: The knob that makes the guitar sound warmer or duller; turning it down drains the bright, trebly part of the signal away and leaves a rounder tone.
fields.purpose_function: It lets a player tailor brightness at the instrument without changing volume; it exists so the tone can be softened for rhythm, jazz, or lead sounds directly from the guitar.
fields.practical_application: A tech verifies the tone pot and capacitor by ear and meter, knowing a smaller cap cuts less treble and a larger one darkens more, and checks for a scratchy pot or failed cap that leaves the control ineffective; typical values are 250k pots with single-coils, 500k with humbuckers, and tone caps around 0.022 to 0.047 microfarads.
common_mistakes: Assuming the passive tone control can add treble when it can only remove it
Thinking pot value does not matter, when 250k versus 500k noticeably changes brightness
Blaming the amp for a dull sound when a rolled-off or faulty tone control is the cause
Confusing a scratchy (dirty) tone pot with a wiring fault
scenario_contexts: Rolling the tone down for a warm jazz archtop sound
Servicing a guitar whose tone knob does nothing because the tone capacitor has failed
Choosing a tone-cap value when rewiring a guitar for a darker or brighter response

sources: Seymour Duncan technical wiring guide (Guitar Wiring 102)

fields.definition: A potentiometer on the guitar wired as a variable voltage divider between the pickup's hot output and ground, with the wiper feeding the output jack; it sets how much of the pickup signal reaches the output, from full level to silence.
fields.plain_english: The guitar's volume knob; it splits off part of the pickup's signal to ground so you can turn the instrument's output up or down without touching the amp.
fields.purpose_function: It gives the player level control at the instrument for swells, for cleaning up an overdriven amp, and for quick muting; it exists so dynamics and gain can be managed from the guitar itself.
fields.practical_application: A tech chooses an audio (logarithmic) taper so the sweep sounds even and knows that rolling the volume down can also dull the highs because of cable capacitance, which is why players fit treble-bleed networks; scratchy pots are cleaned or replaced.
common_mistakes: Fitting a linear-taper pot where an audio taper is wanted, so most of the level change crowds into a small part of the rotation
Not realizing that lowering the volume can also roll off treble due to cable and load capacitance
Assuming a dead output is the pickup when a failed volume pot or jack is the cause
scenario_contexts: Using volume swells for pad-like guitar parts
Backing the guitar volume off to clean up an overdriven amp
Replacing a crackling volume pot during a setup

sources: Seymour Duncan technical wiring guide (Guitar Wiring 102)

fields.definition: The practice of wrapping a hand around the grille or head of a handheld microphone; the cupped hand blocks the rear and side ports that give a directional (cardioid) mic its pattern, pushing it toward omnidirectional, and forms a small resonant cavity that boosts a midrange peak, together sharply increasing feedback and coloring the sound.
fields.plain_english: Cupping your hand around the ball of a mic; it wrecks the mic's directional pattern and creates a honky resonance, which is why it makes live sound squeal with feedback.
fields.purpose_function: It is mainly described as a fault to avoid, because a directional mic relies on unobstructed rear and side ports; some players such as blues-harp performers cup deliberately for a lo-fi tone, but it trades away feedback rejection and neutral response.
fields.practical_application: A live engineer coaches performers not to cup the grille, since it collapses the polar pattern and lowers the gain available before feedback, and recognizes the resulting boxy midrange as a cause of ringing on a vocal mic.
common_mistakes: UNSAFE: Cupping the grille on a loud stage, which collapses the mic's directional pattern and can trigger sudden feedback and hazardous SPL spikes through the PA
Believing cupping makes the mic louder or warmer with no downside
Blaming the mixer for feedback when a cupped mic caused it
Cupping a mic and expecting its rated directional pattern to hold
scenario_contexts: A singer cups the mic and the stage monitors immediately ring with feedback
A blues harmonica player cups mic and harp for a gritty tone while the engineer manages feedback
Explaining to a guest speaker why holding the mic head degrades intelligibility

sources: Shure technical support, Cupping my hands around the microphone head
Ballou, Handbook for Sound Engineers (microphone directional characteristics)

fields.definition: A hollow metal (typically aluminum) mute for trumpet or trombone that seals the entire bell opening with a ring of cork so all of the player's air is forced through the mute; it has a central tube or stem that can be pulled out or left in, and, especially with the stem removed, produces a thin, buzzy, distant timbre rich in upper harmonics, with a wah-wah effect available by opening and closing the hand over the stem cup.
fields.plain_english: The metal cup that plugs a trumpet's bell, made famous by Miles Davis, giving a small, buzzy, far-away sound; covering and uncovering the little tube with your hand makes the classic wah.
fields.purpose_function: It transforms the instrument's tone into a quiet, focused, harmonically bright color used heavily in jazz and film scoring; the cork seal and stem act as an acoustic filter that suppresses the fundamental and emphasizes the upper harmonics.
fields.practical_application: Because a Harmon-muted trumpet is quiet and highly directional, an engineer close-mics it, often just off the axis of the stem, and may add gain and gentle EQ while watching for the piercing high-harmonic wah peaks.
common_mistakes: Confusing the Harmon (metal, cork-sealed, wah-wah) mute with a straight or cup mute
Recording it from a distance when the muted level is low and needs close miking
Forgetting the stem can be removed or adjusted, which changes the tone substantially
Assuming the mute mainly lowers volume rather than reshaping the harmonic spectrum
scenario_contexts: Miking a jazz trumpet using a stemless Harmon mute for an intimate ballad
A brass section using Harmon mutes with hand wah for a big-band effect
Adjusting gain and EQ for the quiet, bright output of a Harmon-muted trumpet

sources: Fletcher & Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments (brass instrument mutes)
